## 1. Scope & Inputs This cycle (i14-2026-10-s4) designs the HOW for three Requirements of the SDLC event service. SDLC-FR-0401 migrates every stored event from the current storage schema to a new one without downtime. SDLC-FR-0402 lets downstream consumers replay stored events of a given type from a chosen point in time, in original order, deterministically and resumably. SDLC-FR-0403 rate-limits submissions per source identifier at 100 submissions per second across all service instances. The normative sources are the three Requirement trees whose fingerprints are listed in the Input Manifest. UX was recorded NOT_APPLICABLE because this is a back-end service only. The current system is treated as one logical service: stateless instances accept event submissions from producers and serve status reads, backed by a single transactional event store. Several million events exist and the migration may run for days. Out of scope, because the Requirements say so: changing the event payload format, consumer registration, and per-tenant quotas. Product decisions the Requirements leave open are listed as product questions and are not answered here. ## 2. Excess submissions from a source over 100 per second receive an explicit rate-limit refusal and are not stored. Other sources' counters are untouched. | The limit applies per source identifier across all instances, which the shared counter store provides
No per-tenant quotas are introduced | Exact window and burst semantics are pending a product question
Fail-open versus fail-closed behaviour when the counter store is unavailable is pending a product question
How the source identifier is established is pending a product question | ## 3. Solution Structure The solution adds five parts to the existing service. First, an Admission Rate Limiter runs in the submission path of every instance and is backed by a shared, replicated low-latency counter store, so the limit holds across all instances. Second, a New-Schema Event Store sits in the same database as the current tables. It holds each event with its unchanged payload, its event type, its acceptance timestamp, and an immutable replay position. Third, a Migration subsystem follows the expand-and-contract pattern. A change-feed Applier mirrors live changes from the old tables to the new tables, so the submission path is not altered during the bulk copy. A Backfill Worker copies historical events. A Verifier compares every event across both schemas. A cutover flag set then moves writes, and afterwards reads, to the new schema, with reverse propagation kept for rollback. Fourth, a single-active Ordering Sequencer stamps replay positions on newly created events in commit order and publishes a stable watermark. Fifth, a stateless Replay API serves cursor-paged replays from a read replica. Replay is enabled only after the migration is verified, because SDLC-FR-0401 states the new schema is the precondition for replay. ## 4. Components & Responsibilities Submission Handler (existing, extended): validates a submission, asks the Admission Rate Limiter for a decision before any persistence, and either persists the event or returns an explicit rate-limit refusal. During migration it writes to whichever schema the cutover flag selects. Status Read Handler (existing, extended): serves status reads from the schema selected by the read flag. Admission Rate Limiter: keys an atomic counter by source identifier in the shared counter store, using a sliding window of 100 submissions per second. Its exact window semantics are pending a product question. It keeps a short-lived local deny cache for sources already over the limit, which cuts round trips during a burst. A refused submission is never persisted. Shared Counter Store: a replicated in-memory key-value store with atomic increment and expiry. It holds only rate-limit counters. New-Schema Event Store: tables for events with a unique event identifier, source identifier, event type, acceptance timestamp, status, byte-identical payload, replay position, and an origin marker (live, applier, backfill, reverse). Indexes support lookup by event identifier, by event type plus replay position, and by event type plus acceptance timestamp. Change-feed Applier: consumes the old tables' commit-ordered change feed and upserts full row after-images into the new tables in feed order. It ignores rows tagged as written by propagation, so changes are not echoed back. Backfill Worker: a single-active, checkpointed, throttled job. It walks old events in original-order-key batches and inserts each into the new tables only if absent. It assigns each historical event a replay position derived from the old original-order key, inside a reserved range below every live position. Verifier: repeatedly scans both schemas, compares a digest of all values per event, reports mismatches, and repairs them from the old schema while the old schema is still the source of truth. Reverse Propagator: after writes move to the new schema, it mirrors new-schema changes back to the old tables for the rollback window. Ordering Sequencer: a single active instance holding a lease. It reads the new tables' commit-ordered change feed, assigns the next live replay position to each newly created event (not to backfilled ones, and not to updates), and advances a published watermark. The watermark is the highest position below which every position is assigned and committed. Replay API: stateless. It resolves a start time to a position, then serves pages of a single event type in ascending position, up to the watermark, with an opaque per-event cursor. ## 5. Interfaces & Data Flows Submission flow: a producer submits an event with its source identifier. The handler calls the limiter, which atomically increments and checks that source's window in the shared counter store. Over the limit, the producer receives the interface's explicit rate-limit refusal (an HTTP 429-equivalent with a retry hint where the interface is HTTP) and nothing is stored. Within the limit, the event is committed to the active schema and acknowledged as today. No other source's counter is touched, so other sources are unaffected. Status read flow: unchanged for clients; the handler reads from the flagged schema. Migration flows: old-table commits go through the change feed to the Applier, which upserts into the new tables. The Backfill Worker moves old historical rows into the new tables with insert-if-absent. The Verifier reads both schemas and reports or repairs mismatches. After write cutover, new-table commits flow through the change feed to the Reverse Propagator and into the old tables. Sequencing flow: new-table creations flow through the change feed to the Sequencer, which writes the replay position and advances the watermark. Replay interface (new, pull-based): a consumer requests a replay with an event type and either a start time or a cursor. With a start time, the API resolves the first position whose ordering attribute is at or after that time. With a cursor, it continues strictly after the cursor's position. Each page carries events in ascending position, each with its own cursor. A consumer resumes by presenting the cursor of the last event it has actually processed, so resumption neither repeats nor skips an event. Because positions are immutable and served only below the watermark, two replays from the same starting point see the same sequence over the range both cover. Replays are independent and server-stateless, so several consumers can replay concurrently. ## 6. Data / Storage One transactional database holds both schemas during migration, so the old and new tables share backups, change feed, and operations. New-schema events are immutable in their original values and payload bytes; only status-type fields change, and only through the normal submission and status paths. Replay positions form a single totally ordered integer space. A reserved low range holds historical events, ordered by the old schema's original-order key. The range above it holds events created after the migration boundary, ordered by the Sequencer from commit order. A position is never reassigned. Secondary indexes on event type plus position, and on event type plus ordering timestamp, serve replay seeks and page scans. The watermark is stored durably beside the Sequencer's checkpoint. Replay reads go to a read replica. The replica carries the watermark in the same replication stream, so a replica never serves a position its replicated data does not yet hold. The shared counter store holds only ephemeral rate-limit windows with expiry and needs no durability. After the contract phase, the old tables are retired once the rollback window closes. ## 7. External Integrations N/A — no third-party systems are involved; producers and consumers use the service's own interfaces described in section 5. ## 8. Security / Authentication / Authorization Submissions and status reads keep the existing authentication and authorization unchanged. The rate limiter keys on the source identifier as established by the existing submission interface. How that identifier is established is a product question: if producers can assert any identifier, one producer could spend another source's allowance. The Replay API sits behind the existing consumer authentication. Authorization of which consumers may replay which event types follows whatever policy the existing service applies to event access; no new policy is defined here. Replay cursors are opaque and integrity-protected, so a consumer cannot forge a position outside the event type it started with. The migration components run with service-internal credentials scoped to the event database and are not reachable by clients. The counter store is reachable only from service instances. ## 9. Deployment / Runtime Model Service instances remain stateless and horizontally scaled behind the existing load balancer. Each instance includes the limiter client and the read and write cutover flags, which are read from shared configuration and can change at runtime without a restart. The shared counter store is deployed replicated, close to the instances, so each admission check costs one low-latency round trip. The event database keeps its primary and gains at least one read replica dedicated to replay, which keeps concurrent replays off the submission path. The Applier, Backfill Worker, Verifier, Reverse Propagator, and Sequencer run as separate single-active workers, each guarded by a lease, with a standby taking over on lease expiry. They can be stopped and restarted at any time because each resumes from a durable checkpoint. The Backfill Worker is throttled against database load so the migration does not degrade submissions over its multi-day run. ## 10. Failure / Recovery Limiter or counter store unavailable: the system either fails open or fails closed, and this choice is a pending product question. Both modes are supported by configuration, and neither is assumed. A counter store failover can lose window state, which at worst admits one extra window of submissions. Applier, Backfill Worker, Verifier, or Reverse Propagator crash: each resumes from its checkpoint. All writes are idempotent (an upsert of the full after-image, or insert-if-absent), so replaying a batch is harmless. Their failures never touch the submission path, so no submission fails because of the migration. Race between backfill and live updates: the Applier upserts the latest full image, and the backfill inserts only if the row is absent, so a backfill row cannot overwrite a newer state. The Verifier catches any residual divergence. Sequencer crash: the watermark stops advancing, so replays reach the watermark and then return empty pages until a standby takes the lease and continues from its checkpoint. Submissions are unaffected, and no position is ever reissued. Replica lag: replays only see positions below the replicated watermark, which preserves the no-skip guarantee. Cutover rollback: until the contract phase, the write and read flags can be flipped back, and the Reverse Propagator keeps the old tables current, so rollback loses no data. Partial write cutover across instances: the Applier keeps draining old-table changes until every instance reports new-schema mode and the old change feed is empty. ## 11. Observability Rate limiting: count of admitted and refused submissions, limiter decision latency, counter store errors, and fail-open or fail-closed activations. Refusals are reported per source as a bounded top-N view, which avoids unbounded metric cardinality. Migration: backfill progress in events and estimated remaining time, Applier lag behind the old change feed, Reverse Propagator lag, Verifier coverage and mismatch count, and submission error rate and latency compared with the pre-migration baseline. Gate criteria for each cutover step are an Applier lag near zero, complete verifier coverage, and zero mismatches. Replay: Sequencer lag between commit and position assignment, watermark age, active replays, page latency, replica lag, and rejected cursors. Each worker exposes liveness and lease ownership. Alerts fire on submission errors attributable to the migration, on any verification mismatch after repair, on watermark stalls, and on limiter store unavailability. ## 12. Migration Implications The migration runs in eight ordered phases, each gated on the metrics in section 11. Phase 1, expand: create the new tables and indexes alongside the old ones; nothing reads or writes them yet. Phase 2, mirror: start the Applier on the old change feed. Record the migration boundary as the point after which every newly created event is observed by the feed. From then on, new creations get live positions from the Sequencer and updates propagate as full images. Phase 3, backfill: copy all pre-boundary events in original-order-key batches with insert-if-absent. Each gets a historical position derived from its original-order key, inside the reserved low range. The copy is throttled and checkpointed, and may run for days. Phase 4, verify: the Verifier compares every event's full value digest across both schemas, repairs from the old schema, and repeats until a full pass reports zero mismatches with the Applier caught up. Phase 5, write cutover: flip writes to the new schema instance by instance. Enable the Reverse Propagator at the same time, which keeps old-schema status reads current. Keep the Applier draining until no instance writes old. Phase 6, read cutover: flip status reads to the new schema. Phase 7, enable replay. Phase 8, contract: after a rollback window with no regressions, stop reverse propagation and retire the old tables. The payload format is never changed. The submission path changes only by flag-selected targets, so no submission depends on a migration component being healthy. ## 13. Architecture Decisions / Trade-offs Decision 1: drive migration propagation from the database's commit-ordered change feed, rather than dual-writing in the submission transaction. Benefit: a fault in the new schema or a mapping error cannot fail a submission, which is the core acceptance criterion of SDLC-FR-0401, and the feed's commit order gives a faithful order for live events. Cost: a change feed is required, and the new schema lags briefly, which is why reads stay on the old schema until verification and write cutover are done. Decision 2: use an immutable replay position assigned by a single-active Sequencer, served only below a stable watermark. Benefit: identical sequences for the same starting point, and exact no-skip, no-repeat resumption even with concurrent commits. Cost: a small replay latency behind live commits, and a single-active component whose failure pauses replay but not submissions. Decision 3: derive historical positions from the old original-order key, in a reserved range below live positions. Benefit: original order is kept across the migration boundary without renumbering. Cost: correctness depends on the old schema having a reliable ordering key. Decision 4: use pull-based, cursor-paged, server-stateless replay. Benefit: concurrent consumers scale on a read replica, and the consumer controls exactly-once processing by choosing which cursor it presents. Cost: consumers must persist their own cursor. Decision 5: use a shared central counter store for rate limiting. Benefit: the limit holds per source across all instances, as SDLC-FR-0403 requires. Cost: one network round trip per submission, and a dependency whose failure behaviour needs a product decision. A local deny cache reduces the load during bursts. Decision 6: keep both schemas in the same database during migration. Benefit: one change feed, consistent backups, and simple rollback. Cost: the backfill competes for the same resources, which the throttle controls. ## 14. Assumptions - The existing service is stateless, horizontally scaled instances over a single transactional event database, and both schemas can coexist in that database during migration. - The event database exposes a commit-ordered change feed that carries the operation type and full row after-images. - The old schema contains a reliable original-order key, such as a monotonic insertion identifier or acceptance timestamp, from which the historical order of events can be reconstructed. - Each stored event has a unique event identifier and an event type attribute within the existing data, so replay by type needs no payload change. - Event payloads and original values are immutable after acceptance; only status-type fields change. - Existing authentication of producers and consumers can be reused for the submission, status, and replay interfaces. ## 15. Risks - If the old schema's original-order key is not strictly reliable, for example because of timestamp ties or a non-monotonic identifier, historical replay order may not match the true original order. — Impact: HIGH - The multi-day backfill competes with submissions for database resources; a throttle set too loosely could raise submission latency or cause timeouts. — Impact: MEDIUM - During write cutover, status reads served from the old schema lag by the Reverse Propagator delay, so a status update can appear briefly stale. — Impact: LOW - Loss or failover of the shared counter store can briefly admit traffic above the limit, or refuse traffic, depending on the pending fail-mode decision. — Impact: MEDIUM - A Sequencer outage stalls the replay watermark; consumers stop receiving new events until a standby takes the lease. — Impact: LOW - If source identifiers are asserted rather than authenticated, a faulty or malicious producer could exhaust another source's allowance. — Impact: MEDIUM ## 16. # SDLC-FR-0401 — Migrate stored events to the new schema without downtime

## Requirement

All stored events must be migrated from the current storage schema to the new one while the service keeps accepting submissions.

## Detailed Behavior

During the migration, submissions and status reads keep working for every producer and consumer. After it, every event is readable in the new schema with its original values.

## Rationale

The new schema is needed for replay, and no outage is acceptable.

## Acceptance / Verification

No submission fails because of the migration; after it, every previously stored event reads back with identical values.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Several million events are stored; the migration may take days.

## Non-Goals

Does not change the event payload format.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0402 — Support event replay for downstream consumers

## Requirement

A downstream consumer must be able to replay stored events of a given type from a chosen point in time, in their original order.

## Detailed Behavior

Replay delivers the same events in the same order every time for the same starting point. A consumer can stop and resume a replay without receiving an event twice.

## Rationale

Consumers rebuild their own state after failures.

## Acceptance / Verification

Two replays from the same point deliver identical sequences; a resumed replay neither skips nor repeats an event.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Several consumers may replay at the same time.

## Non-Goals

Does not define how consumers are registered.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0403 — Limit submissions per source

## Requirement

Submissions must be rate-limited per source identifier so that one source cannot exhaust the service.

## Detailed Behavior

A source that exceeds 100 submissions per second receives an explicit rate-limit refusal for the excess; other sources are not affected.

## Rationale

One faulty producer must not degrade the service for others.

## Acceptance / Verification

A burst from one source above the limit is refused for that source only.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

The limit applies per source identifier, across all instances of the service.

## Non-Goals

Does not define per-tenant quotas.

## Open Questions

None.

First, an Admission Rate Limiter runs in the submission path of every instance and is backed by a shared, replicated low-latency counter store, so the limit holds across all instances. Second, a New-Schema Event Store sits in the same database as the current tables. It holds each event with its unchanged payload, its event type, its acceptance timestamp, and an immutable replay position. Third, a Migration subsystem follows the expand-and-contract pattern. A change-feed Applier mirrors live changes from the old tables to the new tables, so the submission path is not altered during the bulk copy. A Backfill Worker copies historical events. A Verifier compares every event across both schemas. A cutover flag set then moves writes, and afterwards reads, to the new schema, with reverse propagation kept for rollback. Fourth, a single-active Ordering Sequencer stamps replay positions on newly created events in commit order and publishes a stable watermark. Fifth, a stateless Replay API serves cursor-paged replays from a read replica. Replay is enabled only after the migration is verified, because SDLC-FR-0401 states the new schema is the precondition for replay. ## 4. Components & Responsibilities Submission Handler (existing, extended): validates a submission, asks the Admission Rate Limiter for a decision before any persistence, and either persists the event or returns an explicit rate-limit refusal. During migration it writes to whichever schema the cutover flag selects. Status Read Handler (existing, extended): serves status reads from the schema selected by the read flag. Admission Rate Limiter: keys an atomic counter by source identifier in the shared counter store, using a sliding window of 100 submissions per second. Its exact window semantics are pending a product question. It keeps a short-lived local deny cache for sources already over the limit, which cuts round trips during a burst. A refused submission is never persisted. Shared Counter Store: a replicated in-memory key-value store with atomic increment and expiry. It holds only rate-limit counters. New-Schema Event Store: tables for events with a unique event identifier, source identifier, event type, acceptance timestamp, status, byte-identical payload, replay position, and an origin marker (live, applier, backfill, reverse). Indexes support lookup by event identifier, by event type plus replay position, and by event type plus acceptance timestamp. Change-feed Applier: consumes the old tables' commit-ordered change feed and upserts full row after-images into the new tables in feed order. It ignores rows tagged as written by propagation, so changes are not echoed back. Backfill Worker: a single-active, checkpointed, throttled job. It walks old events in original-order-key batches and inserts each into the new tables only if absent. It assigns each historical event a replay position derived from the old original-order key, inside a reserved range below every live position. Verifier: repeatedly scans both schemas, compares a digest of all values per event, reports mismatches, and repairs them from the old schema while the old schema is still the source of truth. Reverse Propagator: after writes move to the new schema, it mirrors new-schema changes back to the old tables for the rollback window. Ordering Sequencer: a single active instance holding a lease. It reads the new tables' commit-ordered change feed, assigns the next live replay position to each newly created event (not to backfilled ones, and not to updates), and advances a published watermark. The watermark is the highest position below which every position is assigned and committed. Replay API: stateless. It resolves a start time to a position, then serves pages of a single event type in ascending position, up to the watermark, with an opaque per-event cursor. ## 5. Interfaces & Data Flows Submission flow: a producer submits an event with its source identifier. The handler calls the limiter, which atomically increments and checks that source's window in the shared counter store. Over the limit, the producer receives the interface's explicit rate-limit refusal (an HTTP 429-equivalent with a retry hint where the interface is HTTP) and nothing is stored. Within the limit, the event is committed to the active schema and acknowledged as today. No other source's counter is touched, so other sources are unaffected. Status read flow: unchanged for clients; the handler reads from the flagged schema. Migration flows: old-table commits go through the change feed to the Applier, which upserts into the new tables. The Backfill Worker moves old historical rows into the new tables with insert-if-absent. The Verifier reads both schemas and reports or repairs mismatches. After write cutover, new-table commits flow through the change feed to the Reverse Propagator and into the old tables. Sequencing flow: new-table creations flow through the change feed to the Sequencer, which writes the replay position and advances the watermark. Replay interface (new, pull-based): a consumer requests a replay with an event type and either a start time or a cursor. With a start time, the API resolves the first position whose ordering attribute is at or after that time. With a cursor, it continues strictly after the cursor's position. Each page carries events in ascending position, each with its own cursor. A consumer resumes by presenting the cursor of the last event it has actually processed, so resumption neither repeats nor skips an event. Because positions are immutable and served only below the watermark, two replays from the same starting point see the same sequence over the range both cover. Replays are independent and server-stateless, so several consumers can replay concurrently. ## 6. Data / Storage One transactional database holds both schemas during migration, so the old and new tables share backups, change feed, and operations. New-schema events are immutable in their original values and payload bytes; only status-type fields change, and only through the normal submission and status paths. Replay positions form a single totally ordered integer space. A reserved low range holds historical events, ordered by the old schema's original-order key. The range above it holds events created after the migration boundary, ordered by the Sequencer from commit order. A position is never reassigned. Secondary indexes on event type plus position, and on event type plus ordering timestamp, serve replay seeks and page scans. The watermark is stored durably beside the Sequencer's checkpoint. Replay reads go to a read replica. The replica carries the watermark in the same replication stream, so a replica never serves a position its replicated data does not yet hold. The shared counter store holds only ephemeral rate-limit windows with expiry and needs no durability. After the contract phase, the old tables are retired once the rollback window closes. ## 7. External Integrations N/A — no third-party systems are involved; producers and consumers use the service's own interfaces described in section 5. ## 8. Security / Authentication / Authorization Submissions and status reads keep the existing authentication and authorization unchanged. The rate limiter keys on the source identifier as established by the existing submission interface. How that identifier is established is a product question: if producers can assert any identifier, one producer could spend another source's allowance. The Replay API sits behind the existing consumer authentication. Authorization of which consumers may replay which event types follows whatever policy the existing service applies to event access; no new policy is defined here. Replay cursors are opaque and integrity-protected, so a consumer cannot forge a position outside the event type it started with. The migration components run with service-internal credentials scoped to the event database and are not reachable by clients. The counter store is reachable only from service instances. ## 9. Deployment / Runtime Model Service instances remain stateless and horizontally scaled behind the existing load balancer. Each instance includes the limiter client and the read and write cutover flags, which are read from shared configuration and can change at runtime without a restart. The shared counter store is deployed replicated, close to the instances, so each admission check costs one low-latency round trip. The event database keeps its primary and gains at least one read replica dedicated to replay, which keeps concurrent replays off the submission path. The Applier, Backfill Worker, Verifier, Reverse Propagator, and Sequencer run as separate single-active workers, each guarded by a lease, with a standby taking over on lease expiry. They can be stopped and restarted at any time because each resumes from a durable checkpoint. The Backfill Worker is throttled against database load so the migration does not degrade submissions over its multi-day run. ## 10. Failure / Recovery Limiter or counter store unavailable: the system either fails open or fails closed, and this choice is a pending product question. Both modes are supported by configuration, and neither is assumed. A counter store failover can lose window state, which at worst admits one extra window of submissions. Applier, Backfill Worker, Verifier, or Reverse Propagator crash: each resumes from its checkpoint. All writes are idempotent (an upsert of the full after-image, or insert-if-absent), so replaying a batch is harmless. Their failures never touch the submission path, so no submission fails because of the migration. Race between backfill and live updates: the Applier upserts the latest full image, and the backfill inserts only if the row is absent, so a backfill row cannot overwrite a newer state. The Verifier catches any residual divergence. Sequencer crash: the watermark stops advancing, so replays reach the watermark and then return empty pages until a standby takes the lease and continues from its checkpoint. Submissions are unaffected, and no position is ever reissued. Replica lag: replays only see positions below the replicated watermark, which preserves the no-skip guarantee. Cutover rollback: until the contract phase, the write and read flags can be flipped back, and the Reverse Propagator keeps the old tables current, so rollback loses no data. Partial write cutover across instances: the Applier keeps draining old-table changes until every instance reports new-schema mode and the old change feed is empty. ## 11. Observability Rate limiting: count of admitted and refused submissions, limiter decision latency, counter store errors, and fail-open or fail-closed activations. Refusals are reported per source as a bounded top-N view, which avoids unbounded metric cardinality. Migration: backfill progress in events and estimated remaining time, Applier lag behind the old change feed, Reverse Propagator lag, Verifier coverage and mismatch count, and submission error rate and latency compared with the pre-migration baseline. Gate criteria for each cutover step are an Applier lag near zero, complete verifier coverage, and zero mismatches. Replay: Sequencer lag between commit and position assignment, watermark age, active replays, page latency, replica lag, and rejected cursors. Each worker exposes liveness and lease ownership. Alerts fire on submission errors attributable to the migration, on any verification mismatch after repair, on watermark stalls, and on limiter store unavailability. ## 12. Migration Implications The migration runs in eight ordered phases, each gated on the metrics in section 11. Phase 1, expand: create the new tables and indexes alongside the old ones; nothing reads or writes them yet. Phase 2, mirror: start the Applier on the old change feed. Record the migration boundary as the point after which every newly created event is observed by the feed. From then on, new creations get live positions from the Sequencer and updates propagate as full images. Phase 3, backfill: copy all pre-boundary events in original-order-key batches with insert-if-absent. Each gets a historical position derived from its original-order key, inside the reserved low range. The copy is throttled and checkpointed, and may run for days. Phase 4, verify: the Verifier compares every event's full value digest across both schemas, repairs from the old schema, and repeats until a full pass reports zero mismatches with the Applier caught up. Phase 5, write cutover: flip writes to the new schema instance by instance. Enable the Reverse Propagator at the same time, which keeps old-schema status reads current. Keep the Applier draining until no instance writes old. Phase 6, read cutover: flip status reads to the new schema. Phase 7, enable replay. Phase 8, contract: after a rollback window with no regressions, stop reverse propagation and retire the old tables. The payload format is never changed. The submission path changes only by flag-selected targets, so no submission depends on a migration component being healthy. ## 13. Architecture Decisions / Trade-offs Decision 1: drive migration propagation from the database's commit-ordered change feed, rather than dual-writing in the submission transaction. Benefit: a fault in the new schema or a mapping error cannot fail a submission, which is the core acceptance criterion of SDLC-FR-0401, and the feed's commit order gives a faithful order for live events. Cost: a change feed is required, and the new schema lags briefly, which is why reads stay on the old schema until verification and write cutover are done. Decision 2: use an immutable replay position assigned by a single-active Sequencer, served only below a stable watermark. Benefit: identical sequences for the same starting point, and exact no-skip, no-repeat resumption even with concurrent commits. Cost: a small replay latency behind live commits, and a single-active component whose failure pauses replay but not submissions. Decision 3: derive historical positions from the old original-order key, in a reserved range below live positions. Benefit: original order is kept across the migration boundary without renumbering. Cost: correctness depends on the old schema having a reliable ordering key. Decision 4: use pull-based, cursor-paged, server-stateless replay. Benefit: concurrent consumers scale on a read replica, and the consumer controls exactly-once processing by choosing which cursor it presents. Cost: consumers must persist their own cursor. Decision 5: use a shared central counter store for rate limiting. Benefit: the limit holds per source across all instances, as SDLC-FR-0403 requires. Cost: one network round trip per submission, and a dependency whose failure behaviour needs a product decision. A local deny cache reduces the load during bursts. Decision 6: keep both schemas in the same database during migration. Benefit: one change feed, consistent backups, and simple rollback. Cost: the backfill competes for the same resources, which the throttle controls. ## 14. Assumptions - The existing service is stateless, horizontally scaled instances over a single transactional event database, and both schemas can coexist in that database during migration. - The event database exposes a commit-ordered change feed that carries the operation type and full row after-images. - The old schema contains a reliable original-order key, such as a monotonic insertion identifier or acceptance timestamp, from which the historical order of events can be reconstructed. - Each stored event has a unique event identifier and an event type attribute within the existing data, so replay by type needs no payload change. - Event payloads and original values are immutable after acceptance; only status-type fields change. - Existing authentication of producers and consumers can be reused for the submission, status, and replay interfaces. ## 15. header.environment: synthetic only: in-memory Fibery fakes, no Fibery API

assumptions: The existing service is stateless, horizontally scaled instances over a single transactional event database, and both schemas can coexist in that database during migration.
The event database exposes a commit-ordered change feed that carries the operation type and full row after-images.
The old schema contains a reliable original-order key, such as a monotonic insertion identifier or acceptance timestamp, from which the historical order of events can be reconstructed.
Each stored event has a unique event identifier and an event type attribute within the existing data, so replay by type needs no payload change.
Event payloads and original values are immutable after acceptance; only status-type fields change.
Existing authentication of producers and consumers can be reused for the submission, status, and replay interfaces.
open_architecture_questions: Does the current event database's change feed retain enough history to cover Applier downtime during a multi-day migration, or is an intermediate durable buffer needed?
What throttle level for the Backfill Worker keeps submission latency within today's observed baseline, as established by a load test against production-like data volume?
Should the replay read replica be dedicated, or can it be shared with other read workloads given the expected number of concurrent replays?

product_questions.detail: Does a replay's original order and chosen point in time refer to the time the service accepted each event, or to a time assigned by the producer? A producer-assigned time allows late arrivals, which would change the sequence returned for an earlier starting point.
Should a replay end at the newest event stored when it starts, or continue into events stored while it runs? The design supports either, as a bound on the watermark.
How is 100 submissions per second measured: as a sliding window, as fixed one-second windows, or with an allowed short burst above 100?

When the shared rate-limit state is unavailable, should submissions be admitted, keeping availability but leaving sources unlimited, or refused, keeping protection but causing an outage for all sources?
Is the source identifier authenticated and bound to the producer, or freely asserted in each submission? This determines whether one source can consume another's limit.
Are all authenticated consumers allowed to replay every event type, or is replay access restricted per type?

risks.detail: If the old schema's original-order key is not strictly reliable, for example because of timestamp ties or a non-monotonic identifier, historical replay order may not match the true original order.
The multi-day backfill competes with submissions for database resources; a throttle set too loosely could raise submission latency or cause timeouts.
During write cutover, status reads served from the old schema lag by the Reverse Propagator delay, so a status update can appear briefly stale.
Loss or failover of the shared counter store can briefly admit traffic above the limit, or refuse traffic, depending on the pending fail-mode decision.
A Sequencer outage stalls the replay watermark; consumers stop receiving new events until a standby takes the lease.
If source identifiers are asserted rather than authenticated, a faulty or malicious producer could exhaust another source's allowance.

sections.architecture_decisions: Decision 1: drive migration propagation from the database's commit-ordered change feed, rather than dual-writing in the submission transaction. Benefit: a fault in the new schema or a mapping error cannot fail a submission, which is the core acceptance criterion of SDLC-FR-0401, and the feed's commit order gives a faithful order for live events. Cost: a change feed is required, and the new schema lags briefly, which is why reads stay on the old schema until verification and write cutover are done. Decision 2: use an immutable replay position assigned by a single-active Sequencer, served only below a stable watermark. Benefit: identical sequences for the same starting point, and exact no-skip, no-repeat resumption even with concurrent commits. Cost: a small replay latency behind live commits, and a single-active component whose failure pauses replay but not submissions. Decision 3: derive historical positions from the old original-order key, in a reserved range below live positions. Benefit: original order is kept across the migration boundary without renumbering. Cost: correctness depends on the old schema having a reliable ordering key. Decision 4: use pull-based, cursor-paged, server-stateless replay. Benefit: concurrent consumers scale on a read replica, and the consumer controls exactly-once processing by choosing which cursor it presents. Cost: consumers must persist their own cursor. Decision 5: use a shared central counter store for rate limiting. Benefit: the limit holds per source across all instances, as SDLC-FR-0403 requires. Cost: one network round trip per submission, and a dependency whose failure behaviour needs a product decision. A local deny cache reduces the load during bursts. Decision 6: keep both schemas in the same database during migration. Benefit: one change feed, consistent backups, and simple rollback. Cost: the backfill competes for the same resources, which the throttle controls.
sections.components_and_responsibilities: Submission Handler (existing, extended): validates a submission, asks the Admission Rate Limiter for a decision before any persistence, and either persists the event or returns an explicit rate-limit refusal. During migration it writes to whichever schema the cutover flag selects. Status Read Handler (existing, extended): serves status reads from the schema selected by the read flag. Admission Rate Limiter: keys an atomic counter by source identifier in the shared counter store, using a sliding window of 100 submissions per second. Its exact window semantics are pending a product question. It keeps a short-lived local deny cache for sources already over the limit, which cuts round trips during a burst. A refused submission is never persisted. Shared Counter Store: a replicated in-memory key-value store with atomic increment and expiry. It holds only rate-limit counters. New-Schema Event Store: tables for events with a unique event identifier, source identifier, event type, acceptance timestamp, status, byte-identical payload, replay position, and an origin marker (live, applier, backfill, reverse). Indexes support lookup by event identifier, by event type plus replay position, and by event type plus acceptance timestamp. Change-feed Applier: consumes the old tables' commit-ordered change feed and upserts full row after-images into the new tables in feed order. It ignores rows tagged as written by propagation, so changes are not echoed back. Backfill Worker: a single-active, checkpointed, throttled job. It walks old events in original-order-key batches and inserts each into the new tables only if absent. It assigns each historical event a replay position derived from the old original-order key, inside a reserved range below every live position. Verifier: repeatedly scans both schemas, compares a digest of all values per event, reports mismatches, and repairs them from the old schema while the old schema is still the source of truth. Reverse Propagator: after writes move to the new schema, it mirrors new-schema changes back to the old tables for the rollback window. Ordering Sequencer: a single active instance holding a lease. It reads the new tables' commit-ordered change feed, assigns the next live replay position to each newly created event (not to backfilled ones, and not to updates), and advances a published watermark. The watermark is the highest position below which every position is assigned and committed. Replay API: stateless. It resolves a start time to a position, then serves pages of a single event type in ascending position, up to the watermark, with an opaque per-event cursor.
sections.data_storage: One transactional database holds both schemas during migration, so the old and new tables share backups, change feed, and operations. New-schema events are immutable in their original values and payload bytes; only status-type fields change, and only through the normal submission and status paths. Replay positions form a single totally ordered integer space. A reserved low range holds historical events, ordered by the old schema's original-order key. The range above it holds events created after the migration boundary, ordered by the Sequencer from commit order. A position is never reassigned. Secondary indexes on event type plus position, and on event type plus ordering timestamp, serve replay seeks and page scans. The watermark is stored durably beside the Sequencer's checkpoint. Replay reads go to a read replica. The replica carries the watermark in the same replication stream, so a replica never serves a position its replicated data does not yet hold. The shared counter store holds only ephemeral rate-limit windows with expiry and needs no durability. After the contract phase, the old tables are retired once the rollback window closes.
sections.deployment_runtime_model: Service instances remain stateless and horizontally scaled behind the existing load balancer. Each instance includes the limiter client and the read and write cutover flags, which are read from shared configuration and can change at runtime without a restart. The shared counter store is deployed replicated, close to the instances, so each admission check costs one low-latency round trip. The event database keeps its primary and gains at least one read replica dedicated to replay, which keeps concurrent replays off the submission path. The Applier, Backfill Worker, Verifier, Reverse Propagator, and Sequencer run as separate single-active workers, each guarded by a lease, with a standby taking over on lease expiry. They can be stopped and restarted at any time because each resumes from a durable checkpoint. The Backfill Worker is throttled against database load so the migration does not degrade submissions over its multi-day run.
sections.external_integrations: N/A — no third-party systems are involved; producers and consumers use the service's own interfaces described in section 5.
sections.failure_recovery: Limiter or counter store unavailable: the system either fails open or fails closed, and this choice is a pending product question. Both modes are supported by configuration, and neither is assumed. A counter store failover can lose window state, which at worst admits one extra window of submissions. Applier, Backfill Worker, Verifier, or Reverse Propagator crash: each resumes from its checkpoint. All writes are idempotent (an upsert of the full after-image, or insert-if-absent), so replaying a batch is harmless. Their failures never touch the submission path, so no submission fails because of the migration. Race between backfill and live updates: the Applier upserts the latest full image, and the backfill inserts only if the row is absent, so a backfill row cannot overwrite a newer state. The Verifier catches any residual divergence. Sequencer crash: the watermark stops advancing, so replays reach the watermark and then return empty pages until a standby takes the lease and continues from its checkpoint. Submissions are unaffected, and no position is ever reissued. Replica lag: replays only see positions below the replicated watermark, which preserves the no-skip guarantee. Cutover rollback: until the contract phase, the write and read flags can be flipped back, and the Reverse Propagator keeps the old tables current, so rollback loses no data. Partial write cutover across instances: the Applier keeps draining old-table changes until every instance reports new-schema mode and the old change feed is empty.
sections.interfaces_and_data_flows: Submission flow: a producer submits an event with its source identifier. The handler calls the limiter, which atomically increments and checks that source's window in the shared counter store. Over the limit, the producer receives the interface's explicit rate-limit refusal (an HTTP 429-equivalent with a retry hint where the interface is HTTP) and nothing is stored. Within the limit, the event is committed to the active schema and acknowledged as today. No other source's counter is touched, so other sources are unaffected. Status read flow: unchanged for clients; the handler reads from the flagged schema. Migration flows: old-table commits go through the change feed to the Applier, which upserts into the new tables. The Backfill Worker moves old historical rows into the new tables with insert-if-absent. The Verifier reads both schemas and reports or repairs mismatches. After write cutover, new-table commits flow through the change feed to the Reverse Propagator and into the old tables. Sequencing flow: new-table creations flow through the change feed to the Sequencer, which writes the replay position and advances the watermark. Replay interface (new, pull-based): a consumer requests a replay with an event type and either a start time or a cursor. With a start time, the API resolves the first position whose ordering attribute is at or after that time. With a cursor, it continues strictly after the cursor's position. Each page carries events in ascending position, each with its own cursor. A consumer resumes by presenting the cursor of the last event it has actually processed, so resumption neither repeats nor skips an event. Because positions are immutable and served only below the watermark, two replays from the same starting point see the same sequence over the range both cover. Replays are independent and server-stateless, so several consumers can replay concurrently.
sections.migration_implications: The migration runs in eight ordered phases, each gated on the metrics in section 11. Phase 1, expand: create the new tables and indexes alongside the old ones; nothing reads or writes them yet. Phase 2, mirror: start the Applier on the old change feed. Record the migration boundary as the point after which every newly created event is observed by the feed. From then on, new creations get live positions from the Sequencer and updates propagate as full images. Phase 3, backfill: copy all pre-boundary events in original-order-key batches with insert-if-absent. Each gets a historical position derived from its original-order key, inside the reserved low range. The copy is throttled and checkpointed, and may run for days. Phase 4, verify: the Verifier compares every event's full value digest across both schemas, repairs from the old schema, and repeats until a full pass reports zero mismatches with the Applier caught up. Phase 5, write cutover: flip writes to the new schema instance by instance. Enable the Reverse Propagator at the same time, which keeps old-schema status reads current. Keep the Applier draining until no instance writes old. Phase 6, read cutover: flip status reads to the new schema. Phase 7, enable replay. Phase 8, contract: after a rollback window with no regressions, stop reverse propagation and retire the old tables. The payload format is never changed. The submission path changes only by flag-selected targets, so no submission depends on a migration component being healthy.
sections.observability: Rate limiting: count of admitted and refused submissions, limiter decision latency, counter store errors, and fail-open or fail-closed activations. Refusals are reported per source as a bounded top-N view, which avoids unbounded metric cardinality. Migration: backfill progress in events and estimated remaining time, Applier lag behind the old change feed, Reverse Propagator lag, Verifier coverage and mismatch count, and submission error rate and latency compared with the pre-migration baseline. Gate criteria for each cutover step are an Applier lag near zero, complete verifier coverage, and zero mismatches. Replay: Sequencer lag between commit and position assignment, watermark age, active replays, page latency, replica lag, and rejected cursors. Each worker exposes liveness and lease ownership. Alerts fire on submission errors attributable to the migration, on any verification mismatch after repair, on watermark stalls, and on limiter store unavailability.

SDLC-FR-0401 migrates every stored event from the current storage schema to a new one without downtime. SDLC-FR-0402 lets downstream consumers replay stored events of a given type from a chosen point in time, in original order, deterministically and resumably. SDLC-FR-0403 rate-limits submissions per source identifier at 100 submissions per second across all service instances. The normative sources are the three Requirement trees whose fingerprints are listed in the Input Manifest. UX was recorded NOT_APPLICABLE because this is a back-end service only. Several million events exist and the migration may run for days. Out of scope, because the Requirements say so: changing the event payload format, consumer registration, and per-tenant quotas. Product decisions the Requirements leave open are listed as product questions and are not answered here.
sections.security_authn_authz: Submissions and status reads keep the existing authentication and authorization unchanged. The rate limiter keys on the source identifier as established by the existing submission interface. How that identifier is established is a product question: if producers can assert any identifier, one producer could spend another source's allowance. The Replay API sits behind the existing consumer authentication. Authorization of which consumers may replay which event types follows whatever policy the existing service applies to event access; no new policy is defined here. Replay cursors are opaque and integrity-protected, so a consumer cannot forge a position outside the event type it started with. # SDLC-FR-0401 — Migrate stored events to the new schema without downtime

## Requirement

All stored events must be migrated from the current storage schema to the new one while the service keeps accepting submissions.

## Detailed Behavior

During the migration, submissions and status reads keep working for every producer and consumer. After it, every event is readable in the new schema with its original values.

## Rationale

The new schema is needed for replay, and no outage is acceptable.

## Acceptance / Verification

No submission fails because of the migration; after it, every previously stored event reads back with identical values.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Several million events are stored; the migration may take days.

## Non-Goals

# SDLC-FR-0402 — Support event replay for downstream consumers

## Requirement

A downstream consumer must be able to replay stored events of a given type from a chosen point in time, in their original order.

## Detailed Behavior

Replay delivers the same events in the same order every time for the same starting point. A consumer can stop and resume a replay without receiving an event twice.

## Rationale

Consumers rebuild their own state after failures.

## Acceptance / Verification

Two replays from the same point deliver identical sequences; a resumed replay neither skips nor repeats an event.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

Several consumers may replay at the same time.

## Non-Goals

Does not define how consumers are registered.

## Open Questions

None.

# SDLC-FR-0403 — Limit submissions per source

## Requirement

Submissions must be rate-limited per source identifier so that one source cannot exhaust the service.

## Detailed Behavior

A source that exceeds 100 submissions per second receives an explicit rate-limit refusal for the excess; other sources are not affected.

## Rationale

One faulty producer must not degrade the service for others.

## Acceptance / Verification

A burst from one source above the limit is refused for that source only.

## Constraints & Edge Cases

The limit applies per source identifier, across all instances of the service.

## Non-Goals

Does not define per-tenant quotas.

## Open Questions

None.

assessment.completeness: All three Requirements are addressed with components, flows, storage, deployment, failure handling, observability and phased migration steps. Product questions are surfaced for the main open WHAT items. Several mechanisms are left unspecified: how the Sequencer distinguishes Applier-created historical rows from genuine new creations; conflict resolution and the old-schema origin marker during mixed-mode write cutover; whether refused rate-limit attempts are counted; the deny-cache lifetime; and the bounds of the reserved historical position range.
assessment.implementability: The building blocks are conventional and implementable on a database with a commit-ordered change feed and full after-images: expand-and-contract migration, change-data-capture propagation, idempotent checkpointed workers, a lease-based sequencer with a watermark, cursor-paged replay and a shared atomic counter store. Implementability depends on unverified assumptions about change-feed capabilities and retention and about a reliable original-order key. The historical-position assignment race and the mixed-mode cutover semantics would need defined behaviour before implementation could meet the replay ordering guarantee.
assessment.internal_consistency: The document is mostly coherent, but some statements conflict. The claim that new positions are assigned only to genuinely new events conflicts with the Applier creating rows for updated pre-boundary events before backfill reaches them. The claim that commit order faithfully orders live events conflicts with instance-by-instance write cutover, where old-path events reach the new tables late. The Applier's echo suppression relies on a propagation tag on old-table rows, while the origin marker is defined only for the new schema. Start-time resolution uses a time attribute, while scan order uses positions that are not monotonic in that attribute.
assessment.source_fidelity: The design stays within the Requirements' WHAT. It keeps the payload format unchanged, introduces no per-tenant quotas and does not define consumer registration. It correctly defers open product decisions instead of answering them. Some stated guarantees exceed what the mechanisms deliver: original order for historical events updated during backfill and for events submitted during write cutover (SDLC-FR-0402); status reads working in every phase (SDLC-FR-0401); and refusal of only the excess (SDLC-FR-0403).
assessment.traceability: The traceability rows cover every selected Requirement with fingerprint prefixes that match the manifest and anchors that exist and are relevant. Constraints and non-goals are reflected. Gaps reference the corresponding product questions and assumptions. The 'how satisfied' summaries assert ordering and availability guarantees more strongly than the design supports, as noted in the findings.

claim_verifications.reason: SDLC-FR-0402 requires replay in original order. The design derives every historical replay position from the old schema's original-order key (tsa-s04, tsa-s06, Decision 3). That key is an unverified assumption (Assumptions, item 3). If the key has ties or is non-monotonic, the immutable historical positions would permanently encode a wrong order, and the Verifier would not catch it because replay positions do not exist in the old schema.

SDLC-FR-0401 states that no submission may fail because of the migration, and that the migration covers several million events over possibly days. The Backfill Worker shares the primary database with the submission path (Decision 6). Its throttle level is not yet determined (open architecture question 1). Resource contention that causes submission timeouts is therefore a real path to violating the acceptance criterion.

The risk is real, but its LOW rating understates it. In Phase 5, writes move to the new schema instance by instance while status reads stay on the old schema until Phase 6. An event newly submitted through a new-schema instance only reaches the old tables after Reverse Propagator delay. During that window it can be entirely absent from a status read, not just stale. SDLC-FR-0401 requires status reads to keep working for every producer and consumer during the migration.

SDLC-FR-0403 requires the limit to hold across all instances, which makes the shared counter store a hard dependency. Window state lost on failover admits excess traffic. If fail-closed is chosen instead, store unavailability refuses all sources. The design leaves the fail mode to a pending product decision (tsa-s10).

Replay is served only below the Sequencer's watermark (tsa-s04, tsa-s10), so a Sequencer outage pauses delivery of new events until lease takeover. SDLC-FR-0402 states no replay latency or freshness bound. Ordering and no-skip guarantees are preserved, so the impact is limited to delay.

SDLC-FR-0403 requires that a burst from one source is refused for that source only. If source identifiers can be freely asserted, one producer can consume another source's allowance, and that other source is then refused. That directly defeats the stated acceptance criterion. The Requirements do not say how the identifier is established.

Both the Applier and the Reverse Propagator depend entirely on the change feed for correctness over a multi-day migration (tsa-s04, tsa-s12). If Applier downtime exceeds feed retention, live changes would be lost from the new schema. The Verifier can repair this only while the old schema is the source of truth. Equivalent loss in the Reverse Propagator after write cutover would compromise lossless rollback. SDLC-FR-0401 requires identical values after migration.

The throttle level is a genuine tuning parameter that the supplied sources cannot determine. It bears on SDLC-FR-0401's no-submission-failure criterion, but it is an implementation calibration, not a structural gap.

SDLC-FR-0402 states that several consumers may replay concurrently but gives no volume. Whether the replica is dedicated or shared is a genuine deployment sizing question that does not affect the correctness of the replay guarantees.

SDLC-FR-0402 refers to 'a chosen point in time' and 'original order' but defines neither the time attribute nor the ordering basis. Service acceptance time and producer-assigned time lead to different ordering keys and different determinism properties for late arrivals. The question is material and the selected Requirements do not answer it.

SDLC-FR-0402 does not say whether a replay is bounded at its start or continues into newly stored events. The determinism criterion concerns identical sequences from the same point, and the design supports either bound through the watermark, so the question is genuinely open but non-material.

SDLC-FR-0403 states '100 submissions per second' without specifying the window type or burst allowance. The choice changes which submissions count as 'the excess', and with it the outcome of the acceptance test. The selected Requirements do not answer it.

SDLC-FR-0403 aims to keep one source from exhausting the service. It is silent on behaviour when the shared limit state is unavailable. Fail-open weakens protection and fail-closed refuses every source. This is a product trade-off the Requirements do not make.

SDLC-FR-0403 keys the limit on 'source identifier' but does not say whether that identifier is authenticated or asserted. The 'other sources are not affected' guarantee depends on the answer, and no selected Requirement supplies it.

SDLC-FR-0402 is silent on replay authorization per event type, and consumer registration is an explicit non-goal. The design defers to existing event-access policy, so the question is real but non-material to the core replay behaviour.

material_unresolved_what.detail: Whether 'original order' and the 'chosen point in time' for replay refer to the service's acceptance time or to a producer-assigned time. This determines how ordering and late arrivals interact with determinism.
How the 100 submissions per second limit is measured: sliding window, fixed one-second windows, or with an allowed burst. This defines which submissions are 'the excess'.
Whether submissions are admitted or refused when the shared rate-limit state across instances is unavailable.
Whether the source identifier is authenticated and bound to the producer or freely asserted. This determines whether one source can consume another source's limit.

new_findings.detail: A pre-boundary historical event can permanently receive a live replay position instead of a historical one. The Applier upserts full after-images of any changed old row, including status updates to events created before the migration boundary. If such an update arrives before the Backfill Worker has copied that event, the Applier's upsert creates the row in the new tables. The Sequencer assigns live positions to 'newly created events' observed on the new tables' feed, so it would treat that row as a creation and give it a live position above every historical position. The Backfill's insert-if-absent then skips the row, so it never gets its historical position. Positions are immutable, and the Verifier cannot detect this because positions do not exist in the old schema. Any historical event updated during the multi-day backfill would therefore be replayed out of original order. The design does not define how the Sequencer distinguishes Applier-created historical rows from genuine post-boundary creations.

Phase 5 write cutover leaves instances writing to both schemas at once, with bidirectional propagation (Applier old→new, Reverse Propagator new→old). Three defects follow. (1) Ordering: an event committed through an old-schema instance reaches the new tables only after Applier lag. A later event committed directly to the new schema can therefore commit there first and receive a lower immutable live position, so original order is inverted for events submitted during cutover. (2) Concurrent status updates to the same event through instances on different schemas can produce lost updates or divergence, and the design defines no conflict resolution. The Verifier is described as repairing only while the old schema is the source of truth. (3) Echo suppression relies on an origin tag, but the old schema defines no such marker. The design also does not say whether the tag is cleared by a later genuine update, so a real old-path update to a reverse-propagated row could be ignored.

Start-time resolution and replay order use different attributes. The Replay API resolves a start time to 'the first position whose ordering attribute is at or after that time' and then scans in ascending position. Live positions follow commit order and historical positions follow the original-order key, and neither is guaranteed monotonic in the time attribute. Under concurrent commits, events with a time at or after the chosen point can hold positions below the resolved position and be omitted. Events with an earlier time can also appear in the sequence. The design does not define replay from a point in time consistently with replay order.

The limiter 'atomically increments and checks' the source's window but does not say whether refused attempts are counted. If they are, a source that sends continuously above 100 per second keeps its sliding window saturated and is refused for all submissions, not just the excess. SDLC-FR-0403 states that only the excess receives a refusal.

The local deny cache for over-limit sources is described only as 'short-lived'. Its lifetime is not tied to the window semantics. A cached deny that outlives the point at which the source falls back within the limit would refuse submissions that are not excess.

The size and upper bound of the reserved historical position range are not specified. The design also does not state how a historical position derived from the old key relates to the Sequencer's first live position, which must lie strictly above every possible historical position. If the old key is a timestamp or a sparse identifier, the derivation into a bounded integer range is not defined.
